title: Equity Value vs Enterprise Value
subtitle: The value that belongs to shareholders differs from the value of the whole operating business
openingQuestion: Equity Value and Enterprise Value - which one is bigger for a company with positive net debt (more debt than cash)?
openingOptions: Equity Value is always bigger in every case
Can't be compared without profit data
Enterprise Value is bigger than Equity Value when the company has positive net debt - because EV adds on the debt that shareholders don't carry directly but which still affects overall value
explanation: Equity Value (= Market Cap for a listed company) is the value that belongs specifically to SHAREHOLDERS. Enterprise Value is the value of the WHOLE operating business, belonging to both shareholders AND creditors. The conversion formula: EV = Equity Value + Net Debt (Debt − Cash). For a company with positive net debt, EV > Equity Value.

diagram.label: Enterprise Value: belongs to shareholders + creditors

realWorldExample.company: Comparing a tech company and a manufacturing company
realWorldExample.description: A tech company typically has lots of cash, little debt → EV can be LOWER than Equity Value. A capital-intensive manufacturing company that typically borrows heavily → EV is usually significantly HIGHER than Equity Value.

quiz.question: When calculating valuation multiples like EV/EBITDA instead of P/E, why must you use EV rather than Equity Value?
options: Because EV always gives a prettier valuation result than P/E does
Because accounting standards require using EV for every valuation ratio
Because EBITDA belongs to every investor so it must match EV
EV/EBITDA and P/E are interchangeable freely, with no rule at all
quiz.explanation: An important valuation principle: the numerator and denominator of a multiple must belong to the same 'scope' of beneficiary. P/E uses Equity Value (share price) against Earnings (profit after interest expense - belonging only to shareholders). EV/EBITDA uses EV (the whole business) against EBITDA (before interest expense).

quiz.question: An analyst mistakenly uses Enterprise Value instead of Equity Value when calculating a P/E ratio (which should properly be P/E = Equity Value / Net Income). How does this mistake affect the result, especially for a company with large debt?
options: This mistake only affects a company that carries absolutely no debt at all
It has no effect at all, since EV and Equity Value are always exactly equal
P/E becomes more accurate when using EV since EV is more comprehensive
P/E is inflated - EV is higher than Equity Value when debt is large
quiz.explanation: This is a classic "mixed scope" mistake in valuation - P/E must use Equity Value (belonging to shareholders) divided by Net Income (profit after creditors have already been paid, also belonging to shareholders); mistakenly using EV (which includes the part belonging to creditors as well) inflates the ratio.

quiz.question: EV is 3,000 billion, debt is 800 billion, cash is 200 billion. What is Equity Value?
options: 2,400 billion (= 3,000 − 800 debt + 200 cash)
3,600 billion (= 3,000 + 800 − 200, both signs wrong)
2,200 billion (= 3,000 − 800, forgetting the cash)
4,000 billion (= 3,000 + 800 + 200, adding everything)
quiz.explanation: Equity Value = EV − Debt + Cash = 3,000 − 800 + 200 = 2,400 billion. Going from EV back to Equity, you reverse the exact two signs used to go the other direction.

quiz.question: Why must EBITDA be paired with EV rather than with Market Cap?
options: Because EBITDA is always larger than net profit so it needs a large denominator
Because EBITDA is cash flow before paying interest to creditors
Because Market Cap can only ever be calculated for a listed business
Because EBITDA is calculated annually while Market Cap is a point-in-time figure
quiz.explanation: The rule is that the numerator and denominator must belong to the same group. EBITDA hasn't had interest expense deducted yet so it belongs to both creditors and shareholders - pairing it with Market Cap is comparing a whole cake to just one slice of it.

quiz.question: Which metric correctly pairs with Equity Value?
options: Revenue, because it reflects the scale of the business
EBITDA, because it's the most commonly used measure
Net profit, because it has already had interest expense deducted
EBIT, because it measures core operating efficiency
quiz.explanation: P/E pairs the share price with net profit - both are what remains for shareholders after creditors have been paid. Revenue, EBITDA, and EBIT all sit above the interest-expense line, so they must be paired with EV.

keyTakeaways: Equity Value: the value belonging to shareholders; Enterprise Value: the value of the whole business
EV = Equity Value + Net Debt (Debt − Cash)
Choose the right type of value (Equity or Enterprise) to match the profit metric used for comparison

practicePrompt.question: When comparing P/E (using Equity Value/Net Income) against EV/EBITDA (using Enterprise Value/EBITDA) between two companies with very different levels of debt, which ratio is fairer, and why?
options: P/E is fairer because Net Income already fully reflects every aspect of the company's operations
EV/EBITDA is fairer, because Enterprise Value is neutral to capital structure
Both ratios are equally fair since both use the same type of business value
Two companies with different debt levels can't be compared by any valuation ratio at all
practicePrompt.explanation: Equity Value: the value belonging to shareholders (after debt is subtracted); Enterprise Value: the value of the whole business (both debt and equity). EV/EBITDA is neutral to capital structure so it's fairer than P/E when comparing companies with significantly different debt levels.

summary.keyIdea: Equity Value: the value belonging to shareholders; Enterprise Value: the value of the whole business
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: EV = Equity Value + Net Debt (Debt − Cash)

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Take the Equity Value and Enterprise Value you just calculated in the two previous lessons, confirm whether the formula EV = Equity Value + Net Debt holds, and whether this company has positive or negative net debt.
application.secondary: Verifying the formula yourself makes the number feel a lot less abstract.

sections.text: Equity Value and Enterprise Value are two of the most commonly confused numbers in valuation - but they answer two completely different questions: one belongs to shareholders, the other belongs to EVERYONE who has put capital into the company.

Equity Value (equal to Market Cap for a listed company) is the value belonging specifically to SHAREHOLDERS. Enterprise Value is the value of the WHOLE operating business, belonging to both shareholders AND creditors. The conversion formula: EV = Equity Value + Net Debt (Debt − Cash). A cash-rich, low-debt tech company usually has an EV lower than its Equity Value; a capital-intensive manufacturing company that borrows heavily usually has an EV significantly higher than its Equity Value.
Why you must choose the right type of value when calculating a multiple

The most important valuation principle: the numerator and denominator of a multiple must belong to the same 'scope' of beneficiary. P/E = Equity Value / Net Income - both belong to shareholders (Net Income is profit after interest has already been paid to creditors). EV/EBITDA = EV / EBITDA - both belong to all investors as a whole (EBITDA is profit before interest, not yet split between creditors and shareholders). If you mistakenly use EV to calculate P/E, the result will be badly distorted - especially severe for a heavily indebted company, since its EV is much higher than its Equity Value.

items: Equity Value → pair with profit metrics belonging to shareholders: Net Income, EPS (→ P/E, P/B)
Enterprise Value → pair with profit metrics belonging to all investors: EBITDA, Revenue (→ EV/EBITDA, EV/Revenue)
Mixing up the two scopes is a classic valuation mistake, especially dangerous for a highly leveraged company
Negative net debt (net cash) makes EV lower than Equity Value

lines: Before calculating any multiple, ask yourself: who does this numerator belong to, and does the denominator belong to that same group?
